docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Five ideas explain how DataStreamDB stores and serves data. Read them in order; each builds on the one before it.

Idea What it answers Instances What is one database, and how do several live in one process? Predicates and schema How is data typed, indexed, and made queryable? Relationships and facets How do nodes point at each other, and how are edges described? Timestamps and transactions When does a write become visible, and what happens on conflict? Namespaces and sharding How do tenants and servers share one deployment?

docs.title: One engine, two deployment modes
docs.text:
The same storage, posting, query, and GraphQL engines run in both modes. The difference is what surrounds them:

  • Standalone adds zero, alpha, raft groups, ACL, namespaces, and HTTP/gRPC frontends. Use it when several processes or tenants need to share data.
  • Embedded opens an Instance inside your process with no servers and no ports. Use it when one application owns its data and wants graph queries without operational surface.

Embedded instances are single-node: one writer, no raft, no ACL, no namespaces. Everything else on these pages — predicates, relationships, facets, snapshots — applies to both modes unless a page says otherwise.

docs.title: Instances
docs.text: An instance is one isolated database: its own storage backend, its own data, its own handle. Nothing is shared implicitly between instances.

docs.title: Two backends
Isolation
docs.text:
Each instance has separate storage, separate schema history, and separate timestamps. Two instances opened from the same configuration still see only their own writes:

const a = new Instance('{}')
const b = new Instance('{}')

a.dqlMutate('{ set { _:x <name> "Ada" . } }')
console.log(a.dqlQuery('{ q(func: has(name)) { name } }')) // Ada
console.log(b.dqlQuery('{ q(func: has(name)) { name } }')) // empty

docs.title: Graph API
docs.text:
DQL and GraphQL run against the instance's posting partition, with their own schema history, GraphQL SDL, and timestamp metadata. Reopening a directory instance restores the data, the schema, and the timestamps together.

The low-level key/value methods (put, get, scan, batch) are a separate storage API for hosts that need raw ordered storage. They are not part of the graph model and are documented in the low-level key/value appendix.

docs.title: Embedded lifecycle
docs.text:
The instance owns the store. Drop the last handle to close it; for directory instances that releases the LOCK. GraphQL subscriptions hold a reference to the engine, so close subscriptions before expecting the directory to be released.

Continue with predicates and schema, or see the language-specific guides: Rust, TypeScript, Python, C.

docs.title: Namespaces and sharding
docs.text: Two different partitions appear in a deployment: namespaces separate tenants inside one database, and groups spread predicates across servers. They solve different problems and can be used together.

docs.title: Namespaces (tenants)
docs.text:
A namespace partitions one instance into tenants. Predicate names carry the namespace on the wire:

Wire name Means 0-name name in namespace 0 (the galaxy) 2-name name in tenant 2

Queries and mutations run inside one namespace; guardians manage all of them. Namespace 0 is the default and can never be deleted. Creating a namespace leases an id from zero, installs the initial schema and types on every group, and bootstraps its guardians.

mutation { addNamespace(input: {}) { namespaceId message } }

Login carries the tenant, and the resulting JWT scopes later requests:

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/login \
  -d '{"userid": "groot", "password": "password", "namespace": 2}'

Namespaces are a standalone feature. Embedded instances are isolated by handle and have no namespace layer — open another instance instead.

See Tenancy for management operations and Security for the ACL side.

docs.title: Groups and tablets
docs.text:
Standalone deployments shard by predicate:

  • A tablet assigns one predicate to a group.
  • A group is an independent raft cluster of alphas with its own data.
  • Zero owns the tablet map and tells alphas where each predicate lives.

GET /state on zero shows the current map. A single-alpha deployment is group 1 serving every predicate.

Sharding is per predicate, not per node. A query that traverses friend and name may touch two groups; the coordinator joins the results.

docs.title: Choosing a layout
docs.text: Situation Layout One application, one process Embedded instance One team, one server Single alpha, group 1 Several teams sharing a cluster Namespaces Dataset larger than one server Multiple groups, tablets spread by predicate Both Namespaces inside each group's predicates

docs.title: What embedded mode leaves out
docs.text: Embedded instances have no zero, no raft, no groups, no tablets, and no namespaces. That is the point: one process owns its data. When those features become requirements, move to the standalone servers; the DQL and GraphQL surface stays the same.

docs.title: Relationships and facets
docs.text: Graphs earn their keep at the edges. DataStreamDB stores relationships as uid predicates and describes each edge with optional facets.

docs.title: Nodes, not lists of strings
docs.text:
A relationship is a node, not a value copied into both records. The difference shows up as soon as the relationship has its own attributes or is shared:

type Movie {
    name
    genre
}
type Genre {
    name
}
genre: [uid] @reverse .

_:matrix <name> "The Matrix" .
_:matrix <datastreamdb.type> "Movie" .
_:scifi <name> "Sci-Fi" .
_:scifi <datastreamdb.type> "Genre" .
_:matrix <genre> _:scifi .

genre is a [uid] predicate. A genre can belong to many movies, be queried on its own, and be traversed in reverse. A string property (genre: "Sci-Fi") would duplicate the label, give the genre no identity, and make reverse traversal impossible.

docs.title: Traversal
docs.text:
Query the edge to read the related node:

{
  movie(func: eq(name, "The Matrix")) {
    name
    genre { name }
  }
}

Declare @reverse to walk the edge backwards:

{
  g(func: eq(name, "Sci-Fi")) {
    name
    ~genre { name year }
  }
}

The reverse predicate is derived from the forward name. It is not a second predicate you declare or write.

docs.title: Facets: properties on the edge
docs.text:
A facet belongs to the relationship, not to either endpoint. Cast roles and billing order are properties of the movie→person edge:

_:matrix <acted_in> _:keanu (role="Neo", billing=1) .

Read them with @facets(...):

{
  movie(func: eq(name, "The Matrix")) {
    name
    cast: acted_in @facets(role, billing) { name }
  }
}

Facet values appear under the alias in the response (cast|role, cast|billing). Without an alias, the predicate name is the prefix (acted_in|role).

Filter on a facet to select edges rather than nodes:

{
  movie(func: eq(name, "The Matrix")) {
    acted_in @facets(gt(billing, 1)) { name }
  }
}

This returns only the cast members whose billing on this edge is greater than one. The person node itself is unchanged; the filter applies to the edge.

Facets are a DQL feature. GraphQL in 0.2.1 does not expose facet syntax — model relationship properties as nodes or as separate predicates when the GraphQL layer needs them.

docs.title: GraphQL relationships
docs.text:
In SDL, an object-typed field is a uid relationship. @hasInverse keeps both sides consistent:

type Movie {
  id: ID!
  title: String @search(by: [term])
  genres: [Genre] @hasInverse(field: movies)
}
type Genre {
  id: ID!
  name: String @id @search(by: [hash])
  movies: [Movie]
}

A nested mutation creates the related nodes and the edges in one operation:

mutation {
  addMovie(input: [{
    title: "The Matrix",
    genres: [{name: "Sci-Fi"}]
  }]) {
    movie { title genres { name } }
    numUids
  }
}

docs.title: Choosing the shape
docs.text:
Question Model Is the target a thing with its own attributes or queries? A node and a uid predicate Is the value only meaningful on this edge? A facet (DQL) or a node if GraphQL needs it Is the relationship one-to-many? A list predicate ([uid]) on the side that points to many Do you need reverse traversal? Declare @reverse

Next: timestamps and transactions.

docs.title: Predicates and schema
docs.text: Data is stored as predicates: named edges from a node to a value or to another node. The schema declares each predicate's type and the indexes that make it searchable.

docs.title: Predicates
docs.text:
A predicate is the smallest unit of structure. name, year, friend, and datastreamdb.type are all predicates. Every fact is a triple:

<subject> <predicate> <object> .
_:matrix  <name>      "The Matrix" .
_:matrix  <year>      "1999"^^<xs:int> .
_:matrix  <genre>     _:scifi .

Subjects are uids (0x2) or blank nodes (_:matrix) that the server maps to uids on write.

docs.title: Schema syntax
docs.text:
name: string @index(exact, term) .
year: int @index(int) .
rating: float @index(float) .
friend: [uid] @reverse .
datastreamdb.type: [string] @index(exact) .
  • The type (string, int, float, uid, …) fixes what a predicate accepts.
  • [uid] and [string] mark list predicates.
  • @index(...) chooses tokenizers; without one, eq/term/range roots cannot use the predicate.
  • @reverse maintains the incoming edge so ~friend works.
  • @count, @upsert, and @lang are also accepted where upstream DQL defines them.

The full type and tokenizer table, with examples for every index, lives in the schema reference.

docs.title: What needs declaring
docs.text:
Mutations auto-derive scalar predicates, Dgraph-style:

{ set { _:a <name> "Ada" . } }

name becomes a scalar predicate: the value is stored and has(name) works with no schema. But it has no index, no UID type, and no reverse edge. Schema is therefore incremental — declare what a query needs, when it needs it.

You want Declare first? Without it Store/read a scalar, has(pred) No The value is stored; has works eq, term, or range roots Yes (@index) The mutation stores; the query fails with attribute ... is not valid scalar type A UID relationship (friend: [uid]) Yes The mutation fails: the predicate is treated as scalar and the UID value is rejected Reverse traversal (~friend) Yes (@reverse) There is no incoming edge to traverse type(Name) root No Matches datastreamdb.type edges; a type declaration adds schema-aware expansion/cascade GraphQL schema Yes (SDL) graphql has no schema; the SDL derives predicates, indexes, and types

You can add schema later. alter is additive, and an index added after data exists is rebuilt over the existing values, so it is queryable immediately.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
A type groups predicates so a node can be selected by what it is:

type Person {
    name
    age
    friend
}

Query it with func: type(Person). Membership is recorded as a datastreamdb.type edge on the node, so the root query works even without a type declaration. The declaration is what makes type-aware expansion and cascade know the type's fields. DQL mutations must set the datastreamdb.type edge explicitly; GraphQL mutations set it automatically.

_:ada <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .

Type declarations require one field per line. type Person { name age } is rejected.

docs.title: Altering
docs.text:
Apply schema with alter; it is additive and idempotent. Adding an index to a predicate that already holds data rebuilds the index over existing values, so the new index is queryable immediately:

budget: int @index(int) .

Removing schema is a separate operation. Standalone servers expose drop_attr, drop_all, and the other drop forms through POST /alter; embedded 0.2.1 supports additive alters only (see Limitations).

docs.title: Where schema lives
docs.text:
Each instance owns its schema. Directory instances persist the alter history and replay it on open, so predicates, indexes, and types survive a restart. Two instances never share schema, even when they point at the same code path.

Next: relationships and facets.

docs.title: Timestamps and transactions
docs.text: Every committed write gets a timestamp. Reads pick a timestamp and see a consistent snapshot as of that point.

docs.title: Standalone servers
docs.text:
A mutation is prepared at a start_ts leased from zero and becomes visible at its commit_ts. The response carries both in extensions.txn:

{
  "data": { "uids": { "ada": "0x2" } },
  "extensions": { "txn": { "start_ts": 41, "commit_ts": 42, "aborted": false } }
}

With ?commitNow=true, the server commits before responding. Without it, the mutation stays pending and you commit explicitly with the returned start timestamp:

curl 'localhost:8080/commit?startTs=41'

docs.title: Conflicts abort
docs.text: If two transactions write the same key, one commits and the other aborts with aborted: true and HTTP 409. The aborted transaction writes nothing. Retry it against fresh data instead of assuming the write landed.

docs.title: Best-effort reads
docs.text: ?be=true skips the timestamp lease and reads whatever is newest. It is faster and can observe a partially applied state, so use it for caches and dashboards, not for decisions that must be consistent.

docs.title: Embedded instances
docs.text:
Embedded mode has one writer and no raft, so there is no cross-node conflict to resolve and no explicit transaction handle:

  • Each dql_mutate or GraphQL mutation commits synchronously at a fresh timestamp before it returns.
  • Each dql_query or GraphQL query reads at the current committed timestamp.
  • The timestamp ceiling is persisted with the instance, so reopening a directory never reuses a timestamp.

There is no API to stage several calls into one transaction. If a group of writes must be atomic, put them in one DQL mutation block:

{
  set {
    _:order <name> "Order #1001" .
    _:order <ordered> _:laptop (quantity=1) .
  }
}

That block commits as one unit.

docs.title: What this buys you
docs.text:
Property Standalone Embedded Snapshot reads Yes, at any leased timestamp Yes, at the current committed timestamp Deferred commit Yes (startTs + /commit) No, mutations commit on return Conflict abort Yes, on overlapping writes Not applicable (single writer) Best-effort reads Yes (?be=true) Not exposed Multi-call transaction Yes No, use one mutation block

Next: namespaces and sharding.

docs.title: Embedding overview
docs.text:
Every embedding goes through an opaque instance handle. Handles are Send + Sync; calls may run on any thread. Dropping the last handle closes that instance only: backend flush, partition close, file-lock release. Graph mutations commit before the call returns.

Language Handle Install Rust Arc<Instance> cargo add datastreamdb-core TypeScript Instance class npm install @datastreamdb/core Python datastreamdb.Instance pip install datastreamdb C datastreamdb_handle_t* release asset: libdatastreamdb_ffi.a + datastreamdb.h

docs.title: What 0.2.1 supports
docs.text:
Capability Embedded 0.2.1 Standalone servers Open multiple isolated instances in one process Yes N/A DQL relationship/pattern queries Yes Yes DQL set/delete mutations Yes Yes Additive schema alters Yes Yes GraphQL queries and mutations Yes Yes GraphQL subscriptions Poll-based Poll/WebSocket Multi-node Raft, ACL, namespaces No Yes

Graph mode is single-node

Embedded DQL/GraphQL runs locally with the same executor as the standalone server. Use the standalone servers for clustering, ACL, namespaces, and WebSocket subscriptions. See DQL and GraphQL for relationship, pattern, schema, mutation, and subscription examples.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Instances open from a JSON object. Unknown fields are rejected so hosts fail fast on version skew.

{ "data_dir": "/var/lib/app/graph-a", "tenant": "default" }
Field JSON type Default Meaning data_dir string path or null null null/omitted = pure in-memory backend. A path = persistent fjall backend. tenant string "default" Label used in logs, metrics, and responses. It is not a data-isolation boundary.
  • One directory per live instance. The persistent backend takes an exclusive LOCK; a second open of the same directory fails until the first closes.
  • Instances are isolated by handle. Two Instance objects never share keys, even when both use the in-memory backend.
  • Use separate instances (and separate directories) for separate tenants or applications.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Embedded 0.2.1 runs the same graph engine as the standalone servers:

Capability Embedded API Schema alters, including index rebuilds dql_alter / dqlAlter / dql_alter DQL set/delete mutations dql_mutate / dqlMutate / dql_mutate DQL relationship and pattern queries dql_query / dqlQuery / dql_query GraphQL schema, queries, mutations set_graphql_schema, graphql Poll-based GraphQL subscriptions graphql_subscribe / graphql_next

There is no separate server, port, or network hop. The instance owns the graph engine and the storage.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
use datastreamdb_core::{Instance, InstanceConfig};

let db = Instance::open(InstanceConfig::memory())?;

db.dql_alter(r#"
name: string @index(exact) .
friend: [uid] @reverse .
type Person {
    name
    friend
}
"#)?;

db.dql_mutate(r#"{
    set {
        _:ada <name> "Ada" .
        _:bob <name> "Bob" .
        _:ada <friend> _:bob .
    }
}"#)?;

let result = db.dql_query(r#"
    { people(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { name friend { name } } }
"#)?;
println!("{result}");

The same calls in TypeScript, Python, and C are on the language pages below. For GraphQL, install an SDL with set_graphql_schema and send documents to graphql; see DQL and GraphQL.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Data is stored as predicates and nodes, exactly as in standalone mode:

  • Scalar predicates auto-derive on first mutation.
  • UID relationships, reverse edges, and indexes need a schema alter. A type declaration adds field awareness for expansion/cascade.
  • type(Name) selects nodes by datastreamdb.type; GraphQL mutations set it automatically.
  • Facets describe an edge, not a node.

The shared model is explained in Concepts. The full type and tokenizer table is in DQL and GraphQL.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Errors are language-native in 0.2.1 — there is no JSON error envelope.

Binding Failure surface Rust Result<_, datastreamdb_core::CoreError> TypeScript thrown Error Python RuntimeError C non-zero status code + datastreamdb_last_error()

Common failures:

  • malformed JSON or unknown request fields (bad request)
  • unknown op
  • invalid config or unknown config fields
  • storage/backend failure
  • opening a persistent directory that is already locked

C status codes: 0 OK, 1 invalid argument, 2 config rejected, 3 engine failure, 4 caught panic.

docs.title: Lifecycle and concurrency
docs.text:
• Rust Instance::open returns Arc<Instance>; clone the Arc for shared use.
  • TypeScript runs blocking engine calls off the JS thread.
  • Python releases the GIL around every engine call.
  • C handles are Send + Sync; datastreamdb_last_error is thread-local.
  • The last close/drop releases the instance’s file lock and flushes its backend.

docs.title: Language guides
docs.text:
• Rust — Instance, DQL and GraphQL, threading, errors.
  • TypeScript — Instance, DQL and GraphQL, envelope calls.
  • Python — Instance, DQL and GraphQL, GIL handling.
  • C — stable ABI, DQL and GraphQL envelopes, buffer ownership.

The low-level key/value methods (put, get, scan, batch) remain available for hosts that need raw storage, but graph applications should use DQL and GraphQL. They are documented separately in Low-level key/value.

docs.title: C embedding
docs.text:
Download the release asset (libdatastreamdb_ffi.a + datastreamdb.h, also checked in at crates/datastreamdb-ffi/datastreamdb.h) and link it:

cc app.c -I. -L/path/to/lib -ldatastreamdb_ffi -lpthread -ldl -lm -o app

If you link the shared library, make it discoverable at runtime:

LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/path/to/lib ./app

docs.title: Open an instance
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

#include "datastreamdb.h"

static int exec(datastreamdb_handle_t *db, const char *request) {
  uint8_t *out = NULL;
  size_t len = 0;
  int rc = datastreamdb_execute(db, (const uint8_t *)request,
                                strlen(request), &out, &len);
  if (rc != DATASTREAMDB_OK) {
    fprintf(stderr, "execute: %s\n", datastreamdb_last_error());
    return rc;
  }
  fwrite(out, 1, len, stdout);
  fputc('\n', stdout);
  datastreamdb_free_bytes(out, len);
  return DATASTREAMDB_OK;
}

int main(void) {
  datastreamdb_handle_t *db = NULL;
  if (datastreamdb_open("{}", &db) != DATASTREAMDB_OK) {
    fprintf(stderr, "open: %s\n", datastreamdb_last_error());
    return 1;
  }

  /* DQL and GraphQL envelopes go here. */

  datastreamdb_close(db);
  return 0;
}

{} opens an in-memory instance. Pass {"data_dir":"/var/lib/app/graph-a","tenant":"app"} for a persistent one.

docs.title: DQL
docs.text:
exec(db, "{\"op\":\"dql_alter\",\"schema\":\"name: string @index(exact) . friend: [uid] @reverse .\"}");

exec(db, "{\"op\":\"dql_mutate\",\"query\":\"{ set { _:a <name> \\\"Ada\\\" . _:b <name> \\\"Bob\\\" . _:a <friend> _:b . } }\"}");

exec(db, "{\"op\":\"dql_query\",\"query\":\"{ q(func: eq(name, \\\"Ada\\\")) { name friend { name } } }\"}");

The C ABI takes JSON envelopes. Build them with a JSON library rather than escaping DQL by hand. DQL type declarations need one field per line, so a multiline schema is sent as a JSON string containing \n.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
exec(db, "{\"op\":\"set_graphql_schema\",\"sdl\":\"type Post { id: ID! title: String @search(by: [term]) }\"}");

exec(db, "{\"op\":\"graphql\",\"query\":\"mutation { addPost(input: [{title: \\\"Hello\\\"}]) { post { id title } numUids } }\"}");

exec(db, "{\"op\":\"graphql\",\"query\":\"{ queryPost { title } }\"}");

GraphQL execution errors arrive in response.errors, not as a failed envelope.

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
exec(db, "{\"op\":\"graphql_subscribe\",\"query\":\"subscription { queryPost { title } }\",\"poll_ms\":100}");
/* Response: {"ok":true,"id":1,"response":{...}} */
exec(db, "{\"op\":\"graphql_next\",\"id\":1,\"wait_ms\":1000}");
exec(db, "{\"op\":\"graphql_unsubscribe\",\"id\":1}");

graphql_next returns {changed, closed, response?}. Close subscriptions when done.

docs.title: Request and response shapes
docs.text: op Request Success response dql_query query {ok:true,data:...} dql_mutate query {ok:true,uids:{...}} dql_alter schema {ok:true} set_graphql_schema sdl {ok:true} graphql query, operation?, variables?, headers? {ok:true,response:{data,errors}} graphql_subscribe query, variables?, headers?, poll_ms? {ok:true,id,response} graphql_next id, wait_ms? {ok:true,changed,closed,response?} graphql_unsubscribe id {ok:true,removed}

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
datastreamdb_execute returns a status code. On failure, inspect the thread-local message:

if (datastreamdb_execute(db, (const uint8_t *)req, strlen(req),
                         &out, &len) != DATASTREAMDB_OK) {
  fprintf(stderr, "execute failed: %s\n", datastreamdb_last_error());
}
Code Name Meaning 0 DATASTREAMDB_OK Success 1 DATASTREAMDB_EINVAL Null pointer, invalid UTF-8, malformed envelope 2 DATASTREAMDB_ECONFIG Config JSON rejected 3 DATASTREAMDB_EENGINE Storage/backend failure 4 DATASTREAMDB_EPANIC Caught Rust panic; instance state unchanged

datastreamdb_last_error() is thread-local and never returns NULL.

docs.title: Ownership and lifecycle
docs.text:
• datastreamdb_open allocates the handle; pass it to datastreamdb_close.
  • datastreamdb_execute allocates the response buffer; release it with datastreamdb_free_bytes(out, len).
  • Closing the last handle flushes and releases the instance’s file lock.
  • Handles are Send + Sync; calls may run on any thread.
  • datastreamdb_last_error is per-thread.

docs.title: Limitations in 0.2.1
docs.text:
• Embedded graph mode is single-node; clustering, ACL, and namespaces require the standalone servers.
  • DQL alters are additive/updating; drop operations and upserts are not exposed.
  • GraphQL subscriptions are poll-based; WebSocket push is not exposed.

See DQL and GraphQL for pattern filters, facets, and subscription shapes. The separate low-level key/value API is available for hosts that need raw storage. A complete reference consumer lives at bindings/c/smoke.c.

docs.title: Low-level key/value API
docs.text:
Graph applications should use DQL and GraphQL. This page documents the raw storage methods for hosts that need a plain ordered key/value store.

The key/value surface uses the default partition; graph data uses the posting partition. They are independent: a put does not create a predicate, and a DQL mutation is not visible through get.

docs.title: Values and keys
docs.text:
Item Supported form Notes Key UTF-8 string Typed APIs take &str; keys sort lexicographically. Value — Rust Arbitrary bytes (&[u8]) Binary-safe. get returns Vec<u8>. Value — TypeScript / Python / C UTF-8 string The JSON envelope only accepts strings. JSON document Serialize to a string/bytes JSON.stringify, json.dumps, or serde_json. Binary data Rust bytes, or base64 string Node/Python/C should base64-encode binary values. Numbers, booleans, dates Encode inside a JSON string No native scalar value types in the KV envelope.

Keys are UTF-8 strings. Use prefixes to model collections:

user:0001
user:0002
post:0001
session:2026-11-25:abc

scan returns keys in lexicographic order. Zero-pad numeric ids when order matters (user:0009 sorts before user:0010).

Rust accepts arbitrary bytes:

db.put("blob:1", &[0x00, 0xff, 0x10])?;

The TypeScript, Python, and C envelopes carry JSON strings. Store structured data as JSON text:

{ "name": "Ada", "age": 36, "active": true }

Serialize before put, parse after get/scan. Do not store raw JSON objects as envelope values; the value field must be a string.

docs.title: Read one key
docs.text:
{ "op": "get", "key": "user:1" }

{ "ok": true, "value": "{\"name\":\"Ada\"}" }

A missing key returns "value": null (Python None, Rust None).

docs.title: Prefix scan
docs.text:
{ "op": "scan", "prefix": "user:", "limit": 100 }

{
  "ok": true,
  "pairs": [
    { "key": "user:1", "value": "{\"name\":\"Ada\"}" },
    { "key": "user:2", "value": "{\"name\":\"Bob\"}" }
  ]
}
  • prefix defaults to "" (scan from the beginning).
  • limit defaults to 1000 and is clamped to 100,000.
  • Results are in key order.
  • There is no cursor in 0.2.1. To page, use a narrower prefix or raise limit; the engine does not return a continuation token.

For large collections, split keys into narrower prefixes (user:2026:11:, user:2026:12:) or store an index key if you need a different access path, e.g. index:email:ada@example.com -> user:1.

docs.title: Write and delete
docs.text:
{ "op": "put", "key": "user:1", "value": "{\"name\":\"Ada\"}" }
{ "op": "delete", "key": "user:1" }

put is an upsert. delete is idempotent; deleting a missing key succeeds.

docs.title: Atomic batch
docs.text:
{
  "op": "batch",
  "puts": [
    { "key": "user:1", "value": "{\"name\":\"Ada\"}" },
    { "key": "user:2", "value": "{\"name\":\"Bob\"}" }
  ],
  "deletes": ["user:3"]
}

The batch is applied atomically. The response reports the number of staged operations:

{ "ok": true, "applied": 3 }

docs.title: Flush
docs.text:
{ "op": "flush" }

flush makes prior writes durable. Dropping the last handle also flushes, but Drop can only log failures; call flush explicitly when the result matters.

docs.title: Typed Rust helpers
docs.text: The Rust API exposes typed helpers beyond the envelope: put, get, scan, delete, delete_range, and write_batch. The other bindings use execute with the envelopes above. See the Rust rustdoc for signatures.

docs.title: Python embedding

docs.title: Open an instance
docs.text:
import json
from datastreamdb import Instance

memory = Instance("{}")
persistent = Instance(json.dumps({
    "data_dir": "/var/lib/app/graph-a",
    "tenant": "app",

docs.title: DQL
docs.text:
import json
from datastreamdb import Instance

db = Instance("{}")

db.dql_alter("""
name: string @index(exact) .
friend: [uid] @reverse .
type Person {
  name
  friend
}
""")

db.dql_mutate("""
{ set {
    _:ada <name> "Ada" .
    _:bob <name> "Bob" .
    _:ada <friend> _:bob .
} }
""")

result = json.loads(db.dql_query("""
  { people(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { name friend { name } } }
"""))
print(result)

docs.text:

docs.title: Threading
docs.text: The GIL is released around every engine call, so one instance can be shared across Python threads. Use a lock only for read-modify-write sequences that must be atomic; the engine does not provide compare-and-swap.

docs.title: DQL and GraphQL queries
docs.text:
Embedded 0.2.1 runs the same DQL executor and GraphQL layer as the standalone servers, but with single-node semantics: no Raft, zero, worker, ACL, or namespaces. Instances are isolated by handle, and graph data lives in the instance's posting partition.

For complete movies, TODO, and orders walkthroughs, see Embedded tutorials.

docs.title: Schema: optional for scalars, required for relationships/indexes
docs.text:
Basic scalar predicates are auto-derived by mutations, Dgraph-style:

{ set { _:a <name> "Ada" . } }

name becomes a scalar string predicate and has(name) works without any schema. But declare schema when you need:

  • UID/relationship predicates (friend: [uid]); otherwise the engine may infer a scalar and reject the UID value.
  • Reverse edges (@reverse) for ~friend traversal.
  • Indexes for eq, term, hash, int, and similar root functions.
  • Type definitions for schema-aware expansion/cascade and GraphQL-derived schemas. The type(Person) root itself matches datastreamdb.type edges.
name: string @index(exact, term) .
age: int @index(int) .
friend: [uid] @reverse .
type Person {
    name
    age
    friend
}

Apply it once per instance (it is persisted for fjall directories):

db.dql_alter(r#"
    name: string @index(exact, term) .
    age: int @index(int) .
    friend: [uid] @reverse .
    type Person {
        name
        age
        friend
    }
"#)?;

db.dqlAlter(`
  name: string @index(exact, term) .
  age: int @index(int) .
  friend: [uid] @reverse .
  type Person {
    name
    age
    friend
  }
`)

db.dql_alter("""
name: string @index(exact, term) .
age: int @index(int) .
friend: [uid] @reverse .
type Person {
  name
  age
  friend
}
""")

C uses the envelope:

{"op":"dql_alter","schema":"name: string @index(exact) . friend: [uid] @reverse . type Person { name\nfriend }"}

docs.title: Relationship data
docs.text:
let assigned = db.dql_mutate(r#"{
    set {
        _:ada <name> "Ada" .
        _:ada <age> "36"^^<xs:int> .
        _:bob <name> "Bob" .
        _:bob <age> "25"^^<xs:int> .
        _:ada <friend> _:bob .
        _:ada <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .
        _:bob <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .
    }
}"#)?;

dql_mutate returns blank-node assignments (_:ada -> uid). GraphQL mutations use the same engine and do not need a separate DQL mutation.

docs.title: Deleting data
docs.text:
Delete blocks take UIDs, so query them first:

{ q(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { uid friend { uid } } }

Delete one relationship edge:

{ delete { <0x2> <friend> <0x3> . } }

Delete every value of a property:

{ delete { <0x2> <age> * . } }

Or delete one exact scalar value:

{ delete { <0x2> <age> "30"^^<xs:int> . } }

Pass these to dql_mutate / dqlMutate / dql_mutate like any other mutation. The reverse edge is removed with the forward edge.

Facets are replaced when the edge is set again; omitted facets are dropped. Setting the edge with no facet map clears all facets. Deleting the edge removes its facets. S * * is not applied in 0.2.1 — delete predicates individually. See deletes for the full rules.

docs.title: Relationship traversal
docs.text:
{
  people(func: eq(name, "Ada")) {
    name
    age
    friend {
      name
      age
    }
  }
}

const result = JSON.parse(db.dqlQuery(`
  { people(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { name friend { name } } }
`))

Reverse edges work with ~friend when the predicate has @reverse:

{ q(func: eq(name, "Bob")) { name ~friend { name } } }

docs.title: Recursive queries
docs.text:
@recurse walks a predicate repeatedly. Put every predicate in one block; nested child blocks are rejected.

{
  chain(func: eq(name, "A")) @recurse(depth: 4) {
    name
    friend
  }
}
  • depth counts levels including the root: depth: 1 returns only the root, depth: 2 adds direct friends, and so on.
  • loop: false (the default) deduplicates edges, so a cycle is traversed once and expansion stops when no new edge remains.
  • loop: true allows revisiting edges and requires depth > 0. Use it when repeated paths in a cyclic graph matter.
  • Omit depth (or set 0) with loop: false for unbounded expansion. The engine stops at the 1,000,000-edge query budget.
  • $depth and $loop variables parse, but embedded 0.2.1 does not expose query variables; use literals. Standalone accepts them in the variables header.

The friend predicate must be declared as [uid] (and @reverse if you need ~friend).

docs.title: Nested pattern filters
docs.text:
{
  q(func: has(name)) @filter(eq(name, "Ada")) {
    name
    friend @filter(gt(age, 20)) {
      name
      age
    }
  }
}

This is a pattern query: the root selects candidates, @filter constrains the root, and the nested friend block applies a second filter to related nodes.

@normalize, @cascade, @ignorereflex, and @groupby are also available. @ignorereflex is a block-level directive: put it on the query block, not on a predicate. See the DQL directives table for the full list.

Other useful roots and filters:

{ q(func: has(friend)) { name } }
{ q(func: uid(0x2, 0x3)) { name friend { name } } }
{ q(func: eq(age, 36)) @filter(has(friend)) { name } }
{ q(func: has(name), orderasc: name, first: 10) { name } }

docs.title: GraphQL schema and queries
docs.text:
db.setGraphqlSchema(`
  type Post {
    id: ID!
    title: String @search(by: [term])
    numLikes: Int @search
    author: Author @hasInverse(field: posts)
  }
  type Author {
    id: ID!
    name: String @id @search(by: [hash])
    posts: [Post]
  }
`)

Mutation and relationship query:

mutation {
  addPost(input: [{title: "Hello", numLikes: 42, author: {name: "Ann"}}]) {
    post { id title numLikes author { name } }
    numUids
  }
}

{
  queryPost(filter: {title: {anyofterms: "Hello"}}) {
    title
    numLikes
    author { name }
  }
}

docs.title: GraphQL subscriptions
docs.text:
Subscriptions are poll-based. The embedded handle captures an initial response, then returns a changed response when the query result changes:

const id = db.graphqlSubscribe(`
  subscription {
    queryPost(filter: {title: {anyofterms: "Hello"}}) {
      title
      numLikes
    }
  }
`)

let event = JSON.parse(db.graphqlNext(id, 0)) // initial: changed=true
db.graphql('mutation { addPost(input: [{title: "Hello again"}]) { numUids } }')
event = JSON.parse(db.graphqlNext(id, 1000))  // changed=true after the mutation
db.graphqlUnsubscribe(id)

graphqlNext(id, wait_ms) blocks up to wait_ms, polling at the subscription interval. It returns {changed, closed, response?}; closed becomes true when the subscription is cancelled or the GraphQL schema is replaced.

In Rust, use the Subscription handle directly:

let sub = db.graphql_subscribe(query, json!({}), &headers, Duration::from_millis(100))?;
assert!(matches!(sub.next()?, SubscriptionEvent::Changed(_)));
let changed = sub.next_timeout(Duration::from_secs(2))?;
sub.close();

docs.text:
• Rust: Result<_, CoreError> (Query, Schema, Posting, GraphQl).

docs.title: 0.2.1 boundaries
docs.text:
• Single-node only; no Raft/zero/worker, ACL, or namespaces.
  • DQL alters are additive/updating; drop operations are not exposed.
  • DQL upserts/conditional mutations and query variables are not exposed yet.
  • GraphQL subscriptions are poll-based; no WebSocket transport.
  • @auth, @custom HTTP/lambda resolvers, remote schemas, and vector indexes are not supported in embedded mode.

docs.text:
[dependencies]
datastreamdb-core = "0.2"
serde_json = "1"

datastreamdb-core returns Arc<Instance>. Clone the Arc to share one instance across threads.

docs.title: Open an instance
docs.text:
use datastreamdb_core::{Instance, InstanceConfig};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // In-memory, isolated instance.
    let memory = Instance::open(InstanceConfig::memory())?;

    // Persistent instance with a tenant label.
    let cfg = InstanceConfig::from_json(
        r#"{"data_dir": "/var/lib/app/graph-a", "tenant": "app"}"#,
    )?;
    let persistent = Instance::open(cfg)?;

    println!("{} {}", memory.id(), memory.backend_name());
    println!("{} {}", persistent.id(), persistent.backend_name());
    Ok(())
}
  • data_dir: null or omitted selects memory.
  • A directory selects fjall and takes an exclusive LOCK.
  • tenant is a label, not an isolation boundary. Use separate instances for separate data.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Instance methods return Result<_, datastreamdb_core::CoreError>:

match db.dql_query("{ q(func: has(name)) { name } }") {
    Ok(result) => println!("{result}"),

docs.title: Share across threads
docs.text:
use std::thread;

let db = Instance::open(InstanceConfig::memory())?;
let mut workers = Vec::new();
for _ in 0..4 {
    let db = db.clone();
    workers.push(thread::spawn(move || {
        db.dql_query("{ q(func: has(name)) { name } }").unwrap();
    }));
}
for worker in workers {
    worker.join().unwrap();
}

Instance is Send + Sync. Clone the Arc rather than opening the same persistent directory twice; the second open fails on the file lock.

docs.title: Quickstart (standalone servers)
docs.text: Start a one-zero, one-alpha cluster, load data, and query it.

docs.title: 1. Build
docs.text:
cargo build --release -p datastreamdb-server

Binaries land in target/release/: zero, alpha, bulk, live.

docs.title: 2. Start zero + alpha
docs.text:
./target/release/zero > /tmp/zero.log 2>&1 &
./target/release/alpha --zero 127.0.0.1:5080 \
  --postings /tmp/datastreamdb-p --wal /tmp/datastreamdb-w > /tmp/alpha.log 2>&1 &
sleep 5
curl localhost:8080/health

Defaults bind zero to 127.0.0.1:5080 and alpha to 127.0.0.1:7080 (gRPC) plus HTTP on 127.0.0.1:8080. Expect {"status":"ok",...} from /health.

docs.text:
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/alter -d 'name: string @index(exact) .'
curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/rdf' -d '_:a <name> "Ada" .'
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/query -d '{ q(func: has(name)) { uid name } }'

Expect Ada back with a 0x… uid.

  '{"query":"mutation { backup(input: {destination: \"/tmp/datastreamdb-bak\"}) { response { code message } } }"}'
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/admin -d \
  '{"query":"mutation { addNamespace(input: {}) { namespaceId message } }"}'

docs.title: Movie graph walkthrough
docs.text: Build a tiny movie database end to end: schema, data, queries, variables, backup, and delete. Every command runs against the Quickstart cluster and is tested in CI against a local zero and alpha.

docs.title: 1. Schema
docs.text:
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/alter -d '
name: string @index(exact, trigram) .
year: int @index(int) .
starring: [uid] @reverse .
director: uid @reverse .
datastreamdb.type: [string] @index(exact) .
type Movie {
  name
  year
  starring
  director
}
type Person {
  name
}'

docs.title: 2. Load movies
docs.text:
curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/rdf' -d '
_:m1 <name> "The Matrix" .
_:m1 <year> "1999"^^<xs:int> .
_:m1 <datastreamdb.type> "Movie" .
_:m1 <starring> _:k .
_:m1 <starring> _:l .
_:k <name> "Keanu Reeves" .
_:k <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .
_:l <name> "Laurence Fishburne" .
_:l <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .
_:m2 <name> "John Wick" .
_:m2 <year> "2014"^^<xs:int> .
_:m2 <datastreamdb.type> "Movie" .
_:m2 <starring> _:k .
'

docs.title: 3. Query it
docs.text:
Keanu's movies through the reverse edge:

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/query -d '{
  keanu(func: eq(name, "Keanu Reeves")) {
    name
    ~starring { name year }
  }
}'

Movies after 2000, ordered by year:

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/query -d '{
  recent(func: gt(year, 2000), orderasc: year) {
    name year
    starring { name }
  }
}'

docs.title: 4. Query with variables
docs.text:
Collect uids in one block, reuse them in another:

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/query -d '{
  var(func: has(year)) { m as uid }
  movies(func: uid(m)) @filter(type(Movie)) { name year }
}'

Conditional writes (cond upserts) guard on these same counts — see DQL upserts.

docs.title: 5. Back up and export
docs.text:
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/admin -d \
  '{"query":"mutation { backup(input: {destination: \"/tmp/movie-bak\"}) { response { code message } } }"}'
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/admin -d \
  '{"query":"mutation { export(input: {format: \"rdf\", destination: \"/tmp/movie-exp\"}) { response { code message } }"}'
ls /tmp/movie-bak /tmp/movie-exp

docs.title: 6. Delete something
docs.text:
curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/rdf' -d '{
    delete { <0x3> <year> * . }
  }'

(Use a real uid from step 3 — 0x3 is illustrative. Deletes need the delete block; bare bodies are always sets.)

You now know the whole loop: DQL for the language, Admin for operations, Security to lock it down.

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text: POST /admin serves GraphQL for cluster operations. With --acl configured the caller must present a guardian JWT (X-DataStreamDB-AccessJWT with the guardians group); without ACL the endpoint is open. Send {"query": "..."} and read data/errors.

docs.title: Health
docs.text: { health { instance address status version uptime } }

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
mutation {
  backup(input: { destination: "/tmp/datastreamdb-bak" }) {
    response { code message }
  }
}

Runs synchronously and reports Success when every group is backed up. destination is a directory or an s3:///minio:// URL; accessKey/secretKey/sessionToken (or anonymous: true for public buckets) authenticate remote destinations. See Backups.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
mutation {
  export(input: { format: "rdf", destination: "/tmp/datastreamdb-exp" }) {
    response { code message }
  }
}

format is rdf (default) or json. namespace selects one namespace (0/omitted is the galaxy); all-namespaces export is not supported yet.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
mutation {
  restore(input: { location: "/tmp/datastreamdb-bak" }) {
    response { code message }
  }
}

Replays the newest backup chain into the live engine. backupId picks a series (empty is latest), backupNum caps it, and encryptionKeyFile decrypts encrypted chains.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
mutation { addNamespace(input: { password: "…" }) { namespaceId message } }
mutation { deleteNamespace(input: { namespaceId: 2 }) { namespaceId message } }

addNamespace leases an id, installs the initial schema, and seeds guardians/groot (default password "password" when omitted). Deleting namespace 0 is rejected. Guardian-only under ACL, like the equivalent gRPC calls. See Tenancy.

docs.title: Backups & export
docs.text: Backups are per-group Snappy-framed streams plus a manifest chain, in the upstream Go on-disk layout, so Go-written and Rust-written backups interoperate. Exports are per-group gzip files (RDF or JSON) plus schema.

docs.title: Destinations
docs.text:
Every operation takes a local directory or an s3:///minio:// URL. Remote credentials come from the request itself:

mutation {
  backup(input: {
    destination: "s3://backups/datastreamdb"
    accessKey: "…", secretKey: "…", sessionToken: ""
  }) { response { code message } }
}

Use anonymous: true for public buckets. Only HTTP endpoints are supported in 0.1.0 (HTTPS needs a rustls build).

docs.title: Backup chains
docs.text: Each run appends one manifest entry: the first run against a fresh destination is a full backup, later runs are incremental. Drops (drop_all, namespace deletes) are recorded in the manifest, so restoring a chain reproduces drops exactly.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
mutation {
  restore(input: { location: "/tmp/datastreamdb-bak", backupNum: 0 }) {
    response { code message }
  }
}

Restore replays newest-series-first back to its full backup, oldest first. backupId selects a series id, backupNum caps how many entries replay (0 is all).

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: Pass --encryption-key-file <16|24|32-byte key> to alpha to encrypt backup streams and export files (AES-CTR, Go wire compatible). Restore reads the key back from the request's encryptionKeyFile (or the server's configured key).

docs.title: DQL guide
docs.text: DQL (the graph query language) over HTTP: schema in POST /alter, reads in POST /query, writes in POST /mutate. This page covers the core; the full language follows the upstream semantics, and anything in Limitations is not implemented.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/alter -d '
name: string @index(exact, trigram) .
age: int .
friend: [uid] .
datastreamdb.type: [string] @index(exact) .
'

Types group predicates for @filter(type(...)):

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/alter -d '
type Person {
  name
  age
  friend
}'

(Type fields go one per line.)

docs.title: Mutations (RDF)
docs.text:
curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/rdf' -d '
_:ada <name> "Ada" .
_:ada <age> "36"^^<xs:int> .
_:ada <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .
_:ada <friend> _:grace .
_:grace <name> "Grace" .
_:grace <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .
'

Blanks (_:ada) come back mapped to uids in data.uids. Without commitNow, commit later with the returned start_ts:

curl 'localhost:8080/commit?startTs=123'

docs.title: Mutations (JSON)
docs.text:
curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '
{"uid": "_:alan", "name": "Alan", "age": 41, "datastreamdb.type": "Person"}'

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/query -d '{
  ada(func: eq(name, "Ada")) {
    uid name age
    friend { uid name }
  }
}'

Root functions include uid(...), has(pred), eq/le/ge/gt/lt, between, allofterms/anyofterms, regexp, type(...), uid_in, and geo functions. Filters, facets, pagination (first:/offset:), ordering (orderasc:/orderdesc:), and @cascade follow upstream semantics.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
All six DQL directives are implemented in both standalone and embedded mode:

Directive Support Notes @filter Yes Functions and boolean operators; nested filters. @normalize Yes Flattens the response to aliased predicates. @cascade Yes Bare or @cascade(pred, ...); checks nested paths. @recurse Yes depth and loop; one level of predicates. @ignorereflex Yes Block-level; removes a node that is its own ancestor. @groupby Yes count, min, max, sum, avg; aliases. 
{ q(func: has(name)) @cascade { name age } }
{ q(func: eq(name, "A")) @ignorereflex { name friend { name } } }
{ q(func: has(age)) @groupby(age) { count(uid) } }

@ignorereflex applies to the query block. Putting it on a predicate (friend @ignorereflex) is rejected. Recursive traversal uses @recurse(depth: N, loop: false) with every predicate in one block; depth includes the root, and loop: true allows cycles and requires a positive depth. See recursive queries for the edge budget and variable rules.

Variables cross blocks with var():

{
  var(func: has(age)) { a as age }
  old(func: gt(age, 30)) @filter(uid(a)) { name }
}

docs.title: Upserts
docs.text:
cond guards a mutation on the request's query vars (eq/gt/lt/ge/le(len(v), n), AND-joined). It shines over gRPC, where one Request carries both query and mutations: the query runs first, its var() counts feed the guard, and failing mutations are skipped without writing.

Note: POST /mutate carries no query, so every len(v) reads 0 there — @if(eq(len(v),0)) always passes and @if(gt(len(v),0)) always fails over plain HTTP. Real upserts need the gRPC query+mutations form.

docs.title: Deletes
docs.text:
Deletes ride in delete blocks (bare bodies are always sets):

curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/rdf' -d '{
    delete { <0x2> <age> * . }
  }'

The delete block takes UIDs or blank nodes, not query functions. Find the UIDs first:

{ q(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { uid friend { uid } } }

docs.title: Delete one relationship
docs.text:
Delete the specific edge by naming both endpoints:

{
  delete {
    <0x2> <friend> <0x3> .
  }
}

The reverse edge (~friend) is removed with it. Deleting one item from a list predicate removes only that edge.

docs.title: Delete all values of a predicate
docs.text:
S P * removes every value of that predicate on the node, including its index entries:

{
  delete {
    <0x2> <age> * .
  }
}

For a scalar, naming the exact value also works:

{
  delete {
    <0x2> <age> "30"^^<xs:int> .
  }
}

For a language-tagged value, include the tag: <0x2> <name@es> * ..

docs.title: Delete every predicate on a node
docs.text:
Dgraph's S * * wildcard is not applied in 0.2.1. The mutation is accepted but leaves the data in place, even on typed nodes. Delete predicates individually with S P *, or drop the predicate server-side with alter.

{ delete { <0x2> <name> * . <0x2> <age> * . <0x2> <friend> * . } }

There is no node-delete operation. Removing all of a node's predicates leaves an empty node; the UID is not reused.

docs.title: Facets
docs.text:
Facets have no separate delete form. The facet map on an edge is replaced when the edge is set again:

{ set { <0x2> <friend> <0x3> (role="Trinity", billing=2) . } }

Omitted facets are removed — setting the same edge with only role drops billing. Setting the edge with no facet map clears all facets while keeping the edge. Deleting the edge removes the facets with it.

Drop a whole predicate, with all its data, via alter instead:

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/alter -d '{"drop_attr": "age"}'

{"drop_all": true} wipes everything (guardians only under ACL).

docs.title: GraphQL data layer
docs.text:
Status in 0.2.1: the GraphQL engine ships as a library (datastreamdb-graphql) and is exposed through embedded instances (set_graphql_schema / graphql / graphql_subscribe). The standalone server has no public /graphql route — the Admin API speaks GraphQL over HTTP. See DQL and GraphQL for embedded examples.

What the crates do:

  • Schema generation: ingest a GraphQL schema, complete it the way the upstream implementation does, and emit the generated DataStreamDB schema + SDL.
  • @auth rules: JWT validation (HS/RS) plus static and RBAC rule evaluation for queries.
  • Resolvers: GraphQL operations rewrite to DQL and execute against datastreamdb-query (queries, mutations with conditions).
  • Subscriptions: a poll-based hub. Embedded instances expose it as a handle (graphql_subscribe / graphql_next); the WebSocket transport is not implemented.

Rustdoc on datastreamdb-graphql is the API reference.

docs.title: HTTP API (alpha :8080)
docs.text: Method + path Purpose GET /health Liveness: status, version, instance, uptime GET /state Membership snapshot (groups, members, tablets, leases) POST /query DQL query body; JSON data + extensions (txn, latency, metrics) POST /mutate RDF body (default) or JSON (by content type); ?commitNow=true commits inline POST /alter Schema text, or JSON drop ({"drop_all":true}, {"drop_attr":"name"}, …) POST /login {"userid","password"} (or refresh_token) → accessJWT + refreshJWT GET /commit?startTs=… Commit one transaction (keys/preds repeat params) GET /abort?startTs=… Abort one transaction POST /admin Guardian-only admin GraphQL (Admin API)

docs.title: Query flags
docs.text: POST /query?ro=true takes a read-only lease; ?be=true reads best-effort at the newest assigned timestamp without a lease; ?startTs=… continues an explicit transaction. Variables travel in the X-DataStreamDB-Vars header as a JSON object.

docs.title: Auth headers
docs.text:
• X-DataStreamDB-AccessJWT: access token from /login (also accepted as X-DataStreamDB-AccessToken). Without --acl every request is open.
  • X-DataStreamDB-AuthToken: legacy shared-secret mode.

docs.title: Mutations
docs.text: Upsert guards ride on ?cond=@if(...); blank nodes (_:a) come back mapped in data.uids. Responses always carry an extensions.txn envelope (start_ts, commit_ts, aborted). See the Quickstart for a full round trip.

docs.title: Zero
docs.text:
zero --my 127.0.0.1:5080 --wal zw --http 127.0.0.1:6080
Flag Default Purpose --my 127.0.0.1:5080 Advertised gRPC address --wal zw Zero group log directory --http / --grpc 127.0.0.1:6080 / 127.0.0.1:5080 Bind addresses --bootstrap true Fresh group vs join --join — Peer zero addrs to join through (with --no-bootstrap) --replicas 1 Alphas wanted per group --heartbeat-ms, --election-ms 100, 1000,2000 Raft timing

Zero serves /health, /state, /assign, /removeNode over HTTP plus the gRPC Zero service.

docs.title: Alpha
docs.text:
alpha --zero 127.0.0.1:5080 --postings p --wal w
Flag Default Purpose --my 127.0.0.1:7080 Advertised gRPC address --zero 127.0.0.1:5080 Zero addrs (comma-separated) --postings / --wal p / w Storage dirs (:memory: for ephemeral postings) --http / --grpc 127.0.0.1:8080 / 127.0.0.1:7080 Bind addresses --group 0 Raft group (0 asks zero to place us) --bootstrap true Fresh group vs join --mutations allow Mutation mode --cache-mb 1024 Posting cache size --acl "" secret-file=…; access-ttl=6h; refresh-ttl=30d; jwt-alg=HS256; empty disables ACL --audit "" output=…; days=10; size=100; empty disables auditing --encryption-key-file "" 16/24/32-byte key for backups/exports --cdc "" file=… change-data-capture sink; empty disables

With --acl, first boot seeds guardians/groot in the galaxy (password password); namespace creation seeds them per tenant.

docs.title: Loaders
docs.text:
bulk data.rdf.gz --schema schema.txt --data-dir p
live data.rdf.gz --data-dir p

Both take RDF/JSON files (plain, .gz, or encrypted + .gz), --batch n-quads per commit, and --encryption-key-file for encrypted inputs. live --alpha is reserved — remote mode is not implemented; loaders write a local engine directly.

docs.title: CDC
docs.text: --cdc file=/tmp/cdc.json appends one JSON event per committed mutation (Go's event shape). Failed sends log and drop; consumers must tolerate gaps after crashes.

docs.title: Security (ACL)
docs.text: Access control is off by default and enabled per alpha with --acl.

docs.title: Enable it
docs.text:
head -c 32 /dev/urandom > /tmp/hmac-secret
./target/release/alpha --zero 127.0.0.1:5080 \
  --acl 'secret-file=/tmp/hmac-secret; access-ttl=6h; refresh-ttl=30d; jwt-alg=HS256'

The secret must be at least 32 bytes for HS256. First boot seeds the guardians group and the groot user (password password) in the galaxy; namespace creation seeds them per tenant.

docs.title: Log in
docs.text:
curl -XPOST localhost:8080/login \
  -d '{"userid": "groot", "password": "password"}'
# {"data": {"accessJWT": "…", "refreshJWT": "…"}}

Send X-DataStreamDB-AccessJWT: <token> on every request. Refresh with {"refresh_token": "…"}. Include "namespace": 2 to log into a tenant (Tenancy).

docs.title: Users, groups, rules
docs.text:
ACL data is ordinary graph data. Create a group with a rule and a user in it (as a guardian):

curl -XPOST 'localhost:8080/mutate?commitNow=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/rdf' \
  -H "X-DataStreamDB-AccessJWT: $GUARDIAN" -d '
_:g <datastreamdb.xid> "dev" .
_:g <datastreamdb.type> "datastreamdb.type.Group" .
_:g <datastreamdb.acl.rule> _:r .
_:r <datastreamdb.rule.predicate> "name" .
_:r <datastreamdb.rule.permission> "6"^^<xs:int> .
_:u <datastreamdb.xid> "alice" .
_:u <datastreamdb.password> "s3cret" .
_:u <datastreamdb.type> "datastreamdb.type.User" .
_:u <datastreamdb.user.group> _:g .
'

Permission bits add up: Read = 4, Write = 2, Modify = 1 (6 is read+write). Rules attach to groups; users inherit their groups' rules.

Enforcement: queries silently drop forbidden predicates, mutations and alters are denied, and guardians bypass all checks. Rule changes apply to new requests once the cache refreshes (committed rule writes trigger it).

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: --audit 'output=/var/log/datastreamdb/audit.log; days=10; size=100' records HTTP/gRPC calls (stdout instead of a path logs to stdout). No output means no auditing.

docs.title: Shortest path
docs.text:
DQL finds a shortest route between two nodes with a shortest root. The root names the two endpoints and one level of predicates to traverse.

{
  shortest(from: 0x2, to: 0x4) {
    friend
  }
}

from and to take UIDs or uid(...) variables. The response contains the route under _path_:

{
  "shortest": [],
  "_path_": [{
    "uid": "0x2",
    "_weight_": 2.0,
    "friend": { "uid": "0x3", "friend": { "uid": "0x4" } }
  }]
}

The _weight_ is the route weight; with no edge weights it counts the edges traversed.

docs.title: Bind the route to a variable
docs.text:
Use an alias and a second block to fetch node properties along the path:

{
  path as shortest(from: 0x2, to: 0x4) {
    friend
  }
  path(func: uid(path)) {
    name
  }
}

docs.title: Options
Rules
docs.text:
• from and to are required and must be UIDs or uid(var).
  • Put every traversed predicate in the single shortest block; expand() is rejected inside it.
  • The search stops at the same 1,000,000-edge query budget as @recurse.
  • Embedded 0.2.1 has no query variables, so use literal UIDs there. Standalone accepts uid(var) endpoints from the variables header.
  • A missing route returns an empty _path_, not an error.

The implementation is Dijkstra for one route and a loopless k-shortest-paths expansion when numpaths > 1.

docs.title: Tenancy
docs.text: Namespaces isolate tenants: predicate names are namespace-predicate on the wire (0-name is name in the galaxy). Guardian-only under ACL.

docs.title: Manage namespaces
docs.text:
Via Admin API:

mutation { addNamespace(input: {}) { namespaceId message } }
mutation { deleteNamespace(input: { namespaceId: 2 }) { message } }

Or via gRPC on api.DataStreamDB: CreateNamespace, DropNamespace, ListNamespaces (a map<uint64, Namespace>).

Creating a namespace leases the id from zero, installs the initial schema/types on every group, and bootstraps guardians/groot inside it. Deleting drops group data first, then tells zero, then records DROP_NS for backups. Namespace 0 (galaxy) can never be deleted.

docs.title: Authenticate into a namespace
docs.text:
Login carries the tenant:

curl -XPOST localhost:8080/login \
  -d '{"userid": "groot", "password": "password", "namespace": 2}'

The access JWT's namespace claim scopes subsequent requests.

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
curl: couldn't connect on :8080. Alpha is still joining. Wait for zero first (curl localhost:6080/health), give alpha ~5s, then check /tmp/alpha.log.

group has no leader / cluster unavailable. Zero is down or unreachable: every timestamp, commit, and tablet lookup goes through it. Restart zero at the same --wal dir and the cluster recovers.

transaction aborted. A conflicting write committed first. Retry the whole read-modify-write at a fresh timestamp; never reuse a start_ts after an abort.

only guardians are allowed to drop all data. /alter drop-all and namespace deletes need a guardian identity under --acl. Log in as groot, or run without --acl.

admin requires guardian (HTTP 403). /admin needs X-DataStreamDB-AccessJWT for a user in the guardians group when ACL is on. Anonymous and non-guardian tokens are rejected — see Security.

Cannot delete default namespace / namespace [0] cannot be deleted. Namespace 0 is permanent, by design.

exporting all namespaces is not supported yet. Pass one namespace (or omit it) instead of a negative id.

docs.title: Embedded
docs.text:
Second open of a directory fails. One live instance per directory: the LOCK file is exclusive. Drop the first handle (after flush) before reopening.

invalid config JSON / unknown field rejected. InstanceConfig rejects unknown fields so version skew fails fast. Only data_dir and tenant exist in 0.2.1.

null from get. Missing keys read as null (TypeScript), None (Python/Rust), or {"value": null} (envelope) — not an error.

docs.title: Reporting bugs
docs.text: Anything outside Limitations that misbehaves is a bug. Report the exact command, its full output, and the tails of the server logs.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
One workspace, ~30 crates. Data flows: clients → frontend (coordinator + HTTP/gRPC) → worker (groups, raft proposals) → posting (storage engine) → store (memory/fjall backends).

Area Crates Embedding datastreamdb-core, datastreamdb-ffi, bindings/{node,python,c} Serving datastreamdb-frontend, datastreamdb-server (binaries), datastreamdb-proto Query datastreamdb-dql, datastreamdb-query, datastreamdb-graphql, datastreamdb-task Storage datastreamdb-posting, datastreamdb-schema, datastreamdb-store, datastreamdb-codec, datastreamdb-tok, datastreamdb-types, datastreamdb-algo, datastreamdb-xidmap, datastreamdb-chunker, datastreamdb-lex Cluster datastreamdb-worker, datastreamdb-raft Ops datastreamdb-backup, datastreamdb-loader, datastreamdb-filestore, datastreamdb-acl, datastreamdb-audit, datastreamdb-enc, datastreamdb-x

Rustdocs for every crate publish to docs.rs. The docs/PROJECT_MAP.md developer map in the repo tracks Go-package parity per crate.

docs.title: Design rules
docs.text:
• Go parity, including limitations, unless a concrete safety or parity reason diverges.
  • Embeddable core: the engine never assumes a server; binaries are thin wrappers.
  • Fail closed: auth failures deny; audit and encryption are explicit flags, never silent defaults.
  • Small files: modules split before ~1000 lines.

Patch release:

  • ACL admin reads now see their own writes; duplicate user and group checks no longer race a just-committed mutation.
  • commit waits for the local applier to reach the commit timestamp before returning, so the next read sees the committed write.
  • Documentation: DQL/GraphQL-first embedded guides, complete per-language tutorial programs, schema and directive references, and a custom landing page.

Embedded graph mode:

  • DQL relationship traversal and nested pattern/filter queries.
  • DQL set/delete mutations with local UID allocation.
  • Additive/updating schema alters with index rebuilds.
  • GraphQL queries and mutations from user SDL.
  • Poll-based GraphQL subscriptions with sync and async helpers.
  • Schema history, GraphQL SDL, and timestamp recovery persisted for fjall directories.
  • Rust, TypeScript, Python, and C-envelope APIs; expanded embedding docs.

Embedded graph mode is single-node. Clustering, ACL, namespaces, WebSocket subscriptions, drop operations, and vector indexes remain server/future work.

First packaged release: DataStreamDB ported to Rust.

Standalone servers (zero, alpha):

  • DQL queries, mutations (RDF/JSON), upserts over gRPC, schema alters, drops, commit/abort.
  • GraphQL admin slice at POST /admin: health, backup, export, restore, addNamespace, deleteNamespace.
  • Multi-tenancy: namespaces with isolated schemas and guardians/groot per tenant.
  • ACL (login, JWT, predicate rules, guardian bootstrap), audit log, backup/export encryption.
  • Backup/restore/export over local dirs and S3/MinIO (HTTP), with manifest chains and drop records.
  • bulk/live loaders, file-sink CDC, multi-zero join.

Embedded:

  • In-process isolated instances from Rust, TypeScript, Python, and C with put/get/delete/scan/batch/flush.
  • In-memory and persistent (fjall) backends.

See Limitations for what 0.1.0 does not do.

docs.title: Limitations (0.2.1)
docs.text:
What is out of scope and tracked for later releases:

  • Embedded graph mode is single-node: no Raft/zero/worker, ACL, or namespaces. Use the standalone servers for those.
  • Embedded DQL scope: relationship/pattern queries, set/delete mutations, and additive schema alters are supported. Drop operations, upserts, and query variables are not exposed yet.
  • DQL deletes: S P * and exact-value deletes work. The S * * wildcard is accepted but not applied in 0.2.1; delete predicates individually. Facets are replaced when the edge is set again — there is no separate facet delete.
  • Embedded GraphQL scope: queries, mutations, and poll-based subscriptions. No WebSocket push, @auth, @custom HTTP/lambda resolvers, remote schemas, or vector indexes.
  • Admin epic remainder: schema/config/user/group mutations, drain, shutdown, async backup tasks with task ids, all-namespaces export, list-backups.
  • S3 HTTPS: HTTP endpoints only; TLS needs a rustls build. Live-MinIO compatibility is unverified.
  • Search: no vector/HNSW indexes.
  • CDC: file sink only (no Kafka); no subscription websocket transport.
  • Storage: no encrypted WAL.
  • Loaders: no remote live-load, no sharded bulk.
  • GraphQL server extras: no JWK fetch, lambda/custom HTTP resolvers, or remote schemas.
  • Testing: no Jepsen runs yet.

Anything else that misbehaves is a bug — report it with the command, its output, and the server logs.

docs.title: Schema reference
docs.text: Predicates, types, indexes, and the query functions each index enables. For the conceptual model, see Predicates and schema.

docs.title: Predicate declarations
docs.text:
name: string @index(exact, term) .
age: int @index(int) .
friend: [uid] @reverse .
datastreamdb.type: [string] @index(exact) .
  • One predicate per line, ending in ..
  • [T] marks a list predicate.
  • @index(...) attaches one or more tokenizers.
  • @reverse maintains the incoming edge (~friend).
  • @count, @upsert, and @lang are accepted where DQL defines them.

Indexing is not allowed on uid, password, or default predicates. uid relationships use @reverse instead.

docs.title: Supported types
docs.text:
Type Stored value Index tokenizers Typical roots GraphQL string UTF-8 text exact, term, fulltext, trigram, ngram, hash, sha256 eq, allofterms, anyofterms, alloftext, anyoftext, regexp, ngram String int 64-bit signed integer int eq, lt, le, gt, ge, between Int, Int64 float 64-bit float float eq, lt, le, gt, ge, between Float bigfloat Arbitrary-precision decimal bigfloat eq, numeric comparisons not exposed bool Boolean bool eq Boolean datetime RFC3339 timestamp year, month, day, hour eq, comparisons, between DateTime geo GeoJSON geometry geo near, within, contains, intersects Point, PointList, Polygon, MultiPolygon uid Reference to another node none; use @reverse uid(...), uid_in, traversal object type password Hashed password none checkpwd not exposed binary Raw bytes none not queryable in the DQL envelope not exposed float32vector Float vector hnsw(...) parses, but the vector engine is a stub in 0.2.1 not queryable not exposed default Auto-derived scalar depends on the derived type has, derived roots mapped from the derived type

There is no separate date type. Use datetime with an RFC3339 value such as "2026-11-30T17:00:00Z"^^<xs:dateTime>.

docs.title: Mutating values
docs.text:
Every type has an RDF literal form. A mutation is a set block; the final . needs a newline (or #) before the closing }.

Type Literal form Example string quoted text "Ada" int xs:int "30"^^<xs:int> float xs:float or xs:double "8.7"^^<xs:float> bool xs:boolean "true"^^<xs:boolean> datetime xs:dateTime (RFC3339) "2026-11-30T17:00:00Z"^^<xs:dateTime> geo geo:geojson "{\"type\":\"Point\",\"coordinates\":[-122.4194,37.7749]}"^^<geo:geojson> uid node reference _:ada <friend> _:bob . or <0x2> <friend> <0x3> . password plain text; hashed on write _:ada <secret> "hunter2" . bigfloat xs:decimal "123.456"^^<xs:decimal> binary xs:base64Binary "hello"^^<xs:base64Binary> float32vector xs:[]float32 reserved; vector mutations are not available in 0.2.1 default any of the above; type is derived "Ada" 
{
  set {
    _:a <name> "Ada" .
    _:a <i> "30"^^<xs:int> .
    _:a <f> "8.7"^^<xs:float> .
    _:a <b> "true"^^<xs:boolean> .
    _:a <d> "2026-11-30T17:00:00Z"^^<xs:dateTime> .
    _:a <g> "{\"type\":\"Point\",\"coordinates\":[-122.4194,37.7749]}"^^<geo:geojson> .
    _:a <big> "123.456"^^<xs:decimal> .
    _:a <bin> "hello"^^<xs:base64Binary> .
  }
}

Pass the block to dql_mutate (Rust), dqlMutate (TypeScript), or dql_mutate (Python), or post it to /mutate on a standalone server.

A Polygon uses the same geo:geojson form:

_:a <g> "{\"type\":\"Polygon\",\"coordinates\":[[[-122.42,37.77],[-122.41,37.77],[-122.41,37.78],[-122.42,37.77]]]}"^^<geo:geojson> .

binary literals are stored as their bytes and returned as a byte array in DQL JSON. password values are stored hashed; verify them with checkpwd.

docs.title: String
docs.text:
name: string @index(exact) .
bio: string @index(fulltext) .
tags: [string] @index(term) .
code: string @index(hash) .
digest: string @index(sha256) .
blob: string @index(trigram) .

{ q(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { name } }
{ q(func: anyofterms(tags, "rust graph")) { tags } }
{ q(func: alloftext(bio, "graph database")) { bio } }
{ q(func: regexp(blob, /matrix/)) { blob } }
  • exact and hash/sha256 are equality indexes.
  • term splits into words; use allofterms/anyofterms.
  • fulltext applies stemming/stop words; use alloftext/anyoftext.
  • trigram supports substring/regexp matching.
  • ngram supports the ngram(...) root.

docs.title: Numeric and boolean
docs.text:
age: int @index(int) .
rating: float @index(float) .
active: bool @index(bool) .

{ q(func: ge(age, 30)) { age } }
{ q(func: between(rating, 7.0, 9.0)) { rating } }
{ q(func: eq(active, true)) { active } }

docs.title: Datetime
docs.text:
due: datetime @index(year, month, day, hour) .

{ q(func: ge(due, "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"^^<xs:dateTime>)) { due } }

Use the date-part tokenizers you need; there is no exact datetime tokenizer.

docs.title: Geo
docs.text:
location: geo @index(geo) .

{ q(func: near(location, [-122.4194, 37.7749], 1000)) { location } }

docs.title: UID relationships
docs.text:
friend: [uid] @reverse .
directed: uid @reverse .

{ q(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { friend { name } } }
{ q(func: eq(name, "Bob")) { name ~friend { name } } }

uid predicates cannot be indexed; @reverse maintains the incoming edge.

docs.title: Password
docs.text:
secret: password .

{ q(func: eq(name, "Ada")) { checkpwd(secret, "guess") } }

docs.title: Vector
docs.text:
embedding: float32vector @index(hnsw(metric: "cosine")) .

The type and directive parse, but the HNSW engine is a stub in 0.2.1: vector mutations and vector search are not available. See Limitations.

docs.title: Type definitions
docs.text:
type Person {
    name
    age
    friend
}

Type fields go one per line. A type groups predicates for schema-aware expansion/cascade; type(Person) roots match datastreamdb.type edges. DQL mutations must set that edge explicitly:

_:ada <datastreamdb.type> "Person" .

GraphQL mutations set it automatically.

docs.title: GraphQL type mapping
docs.text: GraphQL type DQL type ID uid String string Int / Int64 int Float float Boolean bool DateTime datetime Point, PointList, Polygon, MultiPolygon geo [T] list predicate Object type uid relationship

docs.title: Alters and drops
docs.text:
Schema changes are additive by default. Adding an index to a predicate with existing data rebuilds it over that data:

budget: int @index(int) .

Standalone servers also accept drop forms through POST /alter:

{"drop_attr": "budget"}
{"drop_all": true}

Embedded 0.2.1 supports additive alters only.

docs.title: Facets are relationship properties
docs.text:
A facet is a key/value property on an edge, not on a node:

_:matrix <acted_in> _:keanu (role="Neo", billing=1) .

Here acted_in is the relationship, and role/billing describe that specific movie→actor edge. Query them with @facets(...):

acted_in @facets(role, billing) { name }

Facets are a DQL feature. GraphQL in 0.2.1 does not expose facet syntax; model relationship properties as nodes or separate predicates if you need them in GraphQL.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
• DQL type declarations need one field per line.
  • Mutations need a newline or # after the final . before }.
  • Scalar predicates auto-derive; UID relationships, reverse edges, indexes, and types need schema.
  • type(Task) requires datastreamdb.type edges unless the data came from a GraphQL mutation.
  • GraphQL subscriptions are poll-based; see the DQL and GraphQL reference.

rating: float @index(float) .

import json
from datastreamdb import Instance

db = Instance("{}")

# 1. Schema
db.set_graphql_schema("""
type Task {
  id: ID!
  title: String @search(by: [term])
  status: String @search(by: [exact])
  priority: Int @search
  due: DateTime
  project: Project @hasInverse(field: tasks)
  assignee: Person @hasInverse(field: assigned)
}
type Project {
  id: ID!
  name: String @id @search(by: [hash])
  tasks: [Task]
}
type Person {
  id: ID!
  name: String @id @search(by: [hash])
  assigned: [Task]
}
""")

# 2. Add a project and a person
db.graphql('mutation { addProject(input: [{name: "Website launch"}]) { numUids } }')
db.graphql('mutation { addPerson(input: [{name: "Ada"}]) { numUids } }')

# 3. Add a task with nested relationships
added = json.loads(db.graphql("""
mutation {
  addTask(input: [{
    title: "Write release notes", status: "todo", priority: 2,
    due: "2026-11-30T17:00:00Z",
    project: {name: "Website launch"},
    assignee: {name: "Ada"}
  }]) {
    task { title status priority due project { name } assignee { name } }
    numUids
  }
}
"""))
print(json.dumps(added, indent=2))

# 4. Query it
result = json.loads(db.graphql("""
{
  queryTask(filter: {status: {eq: "todo"}}) {
    title status priority due
    project { name }
    assignee { name }
  }
}
"""))
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

mutation {
  updateTask(input: {
    filter: {title: {anyofterms: "release"}},
    set: {status: "doing"}
  }) { numUids }
}
""")
done = json.loads(db.graphql("""
{ queryTask(filter: {status: {eq: "doing"}}) { title status } }
"""))

use std::collections::HashMap;
use datastreamdb_core::{Instance, InstanceConfig};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let db = Instance::open(InstanceConfig::memory())?;

    // 1. Schema
    db.set_graphql_schema(r#"
type Task {
  id: ID!
  title: String @search(by: [term])
  status: String @search(by: [exact])
  priority: Int @search
  due: DateTime
  project: Project @hasInverse(field: tasks)
  assignee: Person @hasInverse(field: assigned)
}
type Project {
  id: ID!
  name: String @id @search(by: [hash])
  tasks: [Task]
}
type Person {
  id: ID!
  name: String @id @search(by: [hash])
  assigned: [Task]
}
"#)?;

    let headers = HashMap::new();

    // 2. Add a project and a person
    db.graphql(
        r#"mutation { addProject(input: [{name: "Website launch"}]) { numUids } }"#,
        None,
        serde_json::json!({}),
        &headers,
    )?;
    db.graphql(
        r#"mutation { addPerson(input: [{name: "Ada"}]) { numUids } }"#,
        None,
        serde_json::json!({}),
        &headers,
    )?;

    // 3. Add a task with nested relationships
    let added = db.graphql(
        r#"mutation {
  addTask(input: [{
    title: "Write release notes", status: "todo", priority: 2,
    due: "2026-11-30T17:00:00Z",
    project: {name: "Website launch"},
    assignee: {name: "Ada"}
  }]) {
    task { title status priority due project { name } assignee { name } }
    numUids
  }
}"#,
        None,
        serde_json::json!({}),
        &headers,
    )?;
    println!("{added}");

    // 4. Query it
    let result = db.graphql(
        r#"{
  queryTask(filter: {status: {eq: "todo"}}) {
    title status priority due
    project { name }
    assignee { name }
  }
}"#,
        None,
        serde_json::json!({}),
        &headers,
    )?;
    println!("{result}");

    // 5. Update it and query again
    db.graphql(
        r#"mutation {
  updateTask(input: {
    filter: {title: {anyofterms: "release"}},
    set: {status: "doing"}
  }) { numUids }
}"#,
        None,
        serde_json::json!({}),
        &headers,
    )?;
    let done = db.graphql(
        r#"{ queryTask(filter: {status: {eq: "doing"}}) { title status } }"#,
        None,
        serde_json::json!({}),
        &headers,
    )?;
    println!("{done}");
    Ok(())
}
